country.comment: Study conducted in 8 settlements in Ngamiland district, north-west Botswana.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 2.1

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive quantitative cross-tabulations and qualitative institutional findings reported; only income differences across settlement categories report a p-value (p = 0.00), while access and water-security outcomes are reported as proportions and administrative counts without regression CIs.
effect_estimate.value: Statutory settlement recognition (gazetted vs. ungazetted status) governs entitlement to public water supply: across N = 554 surveyed households in 8 settlements, 88% (predominantly in gazetted settlements) used improved water sources (46.8% yard taps, 23.1% communal water points, 10.8% indoor taps, 7.2% neighbor's taps) while 12% (mainly in ungazetted settlements) used unprotected sources, with 100% of households in unserved ungazetted settlements (Gucha, Samedupi, Xobe) relying on unprotected rivers/streams and experiencing water security problems. Political discretion created uneven exceptions: ward councilors secured connections for 30 ungazetted settlements along transmission lines (including Ukusi), whereas the North-West District Council (NWDC) refused to connect ungazetted Gucha along the same line. Overall, 74% of surveyed households experienced water security problems in the prior 12 months, 31% lacked water from their main source at survey, 51% in Maun faced acute shortages in the prior 24 hours, and 100% in Matlapana and Somelo lacked main-source water since 2009. Institutional fragmentation between DWA and NWDC prevented connecting water-deprived Matlapana to a passing DWA pipeline; DWA ceased repairing communal taps (0 working in Maun; 2 of 10 in Matlapana) to encourage private connections and began disconnecting defaulting Maun households in July 2012 over BWP 2,708,428 in arrears (whereas NWDC councilors blocked rural disconnections); unplanned residential stand layouts left 32% of Maun outside distribution network coverage; and monthly household income restricting private-connection affordability differed significantly across settlements (p = 0.00).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 5-7, Sections 3.1-3.4.1 & Figs. 2-3; PDF pp. 9-12, Sections 3.5.2-3.8 & Tables 4, 7

mechanism_certainty.comment: Mixed-methods design (MMAT ceiling = 2). Assigned 2 because primary fieldwork (key informant interviews with DWA/NWDC officials and councilors, household survey, focus groups, participant observation and agency records) directly documents the legal and administrative mechanisms operating on water access (statutory exclusion of ungazetted settlements, NWDC connection refusals vs. political councilor exceptions, DWA cessation of communal tap repairs and arrears disconnections, and DWA/NWDC institutional fragmentation).

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines statutory gazetted/ungazetted settlement recognition and catchment thresholds (ELIGIBILITY, service_area, planning), unplanned residential plot layouts impeding network coverage (planning), subsidized vs. cost-recovery WUC tariffs (BURDEN, fees), political intervention by councilors to connect 30 ungazetted settlements vs. NWDC refusal for Gucha and councilor resistance to disconnections (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, discretion, accommodation, political_coordination), lack of resident consultation on WUC takeover and resident petition/protest (participation, complaint), DWA disconnections for non-payment vs. NWDC non-enforcement (ENFORCEMENT, disconnection), and uncoordinated statutes and parallel DWA/NWDC mandates (institutional_fragmentation).
